facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
The applicants in the Chrysostomos and Papachrysostomou v. Turkey case also took part in the demonstration of 19 July 1989 in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
The applicant in the Loizidou v. Turkey case also took part in the demonstration of 19 July 1989 in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held on the fifteenth anniversary of the Turkish intervention in Cyprus.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held in support of the missing persons and to protest against human rights violations.
The applicant joined the demonstration of 19 July 1989 as a reporter for the newspaper Exormisis.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.

In his report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

Before the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court passed sentence, the Bishop of Kitium, speaking on behalf of all the accused, made a statement saying that their struggle was peaceful, that their aim was to encourage Greek and Turkish-Cypriots to live together in peace, that they carried no weapons and that they had asked for UN protection.
During the demonstration of 19 July 1989, dozens of armed Turkish policemen and soldiers moved towards the demonstrators.
While the applicant was trying to help some of the women demonstrators, he was grabbed and beaten by Turkish policemen.
The applicant was hit in the face and other parts of the body by Turkish policemen during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant was taken at gunpoint together with others who had also been arrested during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant's photographic equipment was seized despite him showing his press card during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant was led to a bus through an angry crowd of 200-300 civilians who shouted abuse and threats at him.
As the applicant was walking without police protection, the crowd had an opportunity to rush at him, and he was dragged and beaten until two policemen came and accompanied him onto the bus.
The applicant was transported to the so-called "Pavlides Garage", where a body search was carried out and all his personal effects were taken.
At around 2.30 a.m. on 20 July 1989, the applicant and some other men were ordered onto a police bus.
The applicant was taken to the Seray Police Station, where, after a body search, he was held in a cell that was filthy, dirty and dark.
At around 2.00 p.m. on 20 July 1989, the applicant was given back his personal effects and taken to court together with seven other prisoners.
The applicant was remanded in custody for two days following the court hearing on 20 July 1989.
On 22 July 1989, the applicant was sentenced to three days' imprisonment and a fine of 50 Cypriot pounds (CYP) – approximately 85 euros (EUR).
The sentence imposed on the applicant on 22 July 1989 included five additional days in prison in default of payment of the fine within 24 hours.
The applicant was detained in Ortakeuy Prison from 24 until 28 July 1989.
On 28 July 1989, the applicant was released in front of journalists and television cameras.

The English translation of the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering "TRNC" territory without permission, contrary to sections 2, 8 and 9 of Law no. 5/72.

The English translation of the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering "TRNC" territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the "Green Line" in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the "TRNC".
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the events created considerable tension in the island and that intensive efforts were made, both at the UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that on 21 July 1989, he expressed his concern at the events and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UN buffer zone as well as their responsibility to ensure that that area was not violated.

In support of his claim of ill-treatment, the applicant produced five medical certificates.

A certificate issued on 16 December 2002 by Dr. Andreas G. Constantinides, consultant surgeon at the Evangelistria Medical Centre in Nicosia, stated that Mr Tasos Asproftas (the applicant) is suffering from osteoarthritis of the cervical cord and that Dr. Constantinides recommended he stay at home and undergo physiotherapy from 17 December until 28 December 2002.

A certificate issued on an unspecified date by Dr. S.C. Sergiou, orthopaedic surgeon in Larnaka, stated that Mr Tasos Asproftas (the applicant) is suffering from cervical disc disease and is unable to work from 3 January 2003 until 12 January 2003.

A certificate issued on 9 January 2003 by the medical and public health services – X-rays department – of the Republic of Cyprus stated that Mr Tasos Asproftas (the applicant) had a rear central hernia of the disc, rear lateral right osteophyte in the area of chronic hernia of the disc A4-A5, rear lateral left osteophyte in the area of chronic hernia in discs A5-A6 and A6-A7, straight cervical spine due to muscles' spasm, and stenosis of the middle sections of the spinal cord A4-A5 and A5-A6.

A certificate issued on an unspecified date by Dr. Nicos Chr. Spanos, neurosurgeon in Nicosia, recommended that Mr Asproftas (the applicant) be granted sick leave from 13 January 2003 until 31 January 2003 for investigation and treatment of the cervical middle spinal disc.

A certificate issued on 7 February 2003 by Dr. Nicolas C. Christodoulou, specialist in physical medicine and rehabilitation sport medicine in Limassol, diagnosed Mr Asproftas (the applicant) with severe left cervicobranchial syndrome (radiculitis C7) and instructed approximately 12 sessions of physiotherapy including interferential current, short wave diathermy, and mild cervical massage.

The applicant alleged that his health problems (osteoarthritis of the cervical cord, cervical disc disease, and related conditions) were the result of the savage blows he had received from Turkish policemen, soldiers and civilians in July 1989.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The Government alleged that no one was ill-treated during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that a short while later, Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women.
The final set of photographs produced by the applicant show members of the Turkish-Cypriot police using force to arrest some of the women demonstrators during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.

The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court noted that the applicant stated that he was a journalist, that he had been arrested while he was following the demonstration even though the peacekeeping forces had given him permission to do so.

In deciding on the sentence, the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court took into account the seriousness of the offence and the fact that the accused had shown no remorse and continued to deny the validity of the "TRNC".
